nameStory: White deadnettle earned its name because it looks remarkably like stinging nettle but completely lacks the stinging hairs - it's 'dead' to the touch! The 'white' part comes from its pure white flowers that bloom in clusters along the stem. Early herbalists called plants like this 'dead' nettles because they were safe imposters of their painful cousins.
description: White deadnettle is a low-growing perennial herb that spreads along the ground, reaching about 8-24 inches tall. It has heart-shaped, serrated leaves arranged in pairs along square stems, and produces clusters of white, hooded flowers that look like tiny snapdragons. As a member of the mint family, it has the characteristic square stem, though it lacks the strong minty scent of its relatives. The plant forms spreading patches through underground runners.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white, hooded flowers cluster in whorls around the stem where leaves attach. Each flower is tubular with a distinctive hood-like upper lip and smaller lower lip, about 3/4 inch long.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips and toothed edges, arranged in opposite pairs. They're soft to touch, wrinkled-looking with prominent veins, and completely harmless unlike stinging nettle.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with stems that root at joints where they touch the ground. Plants stay relatively short but can spread several feet wide.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel hollow and are covered in soft, fine hairs. Roll the stem between your fingers to feel the distinct four-sided shape typical of mint family plants.

habitat: Look for white deadnettle in disturbed soils around gardens, roadsides, and waste areas, though it's quite rare in New England with only 6 recorded observations. It prefers moist, fertile soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. When found, it's often growing near other weedy species in areas with rich, nitrogen-rich soil.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, looking fresh and bright green. Flowering typically begins in late spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with white flowers most abundant. Look for the characteristic hooded flowers clustered around stem joints.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall. Leaves remain green longer than many other herbaceous plants, persisting until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only underground runners. Look for dead stems and last year's growth in protected areas.

funFact: White deadnettle flowers are designed like tiny landing pads for bees - the lower lip provides a perfect platform while the bee crawls inside the hood to reach nectar, getting dusted with pollen in the process!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with stinging nettle, but white deadnettle has opposite leaves (stinging nettle's are alternate) and completely lacks stinging hairs. Memory trick: 'Dead means safe to touch, opposite leaves give it away.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'nettle,' white deadnettle is actually in the mint family and completely unrelated to true nettles. This is a classic example of common names being misleading - the resemblance is purely superficial.
compareHints: White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit. Red deadnettle and henbit have purplish flowers and are annuals, while yellow archangel has yellow blooms. Spotted deadnettle has white flowers with purple spots, making white deadnettle's unmarked blooms distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color.
Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants.

Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers.
Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves.
Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones.
